terms.plain: The idea that a dollar today is worth more than the same dollar later, so you cannot compare amounts of money without knowing when each one arrives.
terms.formal: The principle that money available now is worth more than an identical sum in the future, because of its earning capacity, the risk that the future payment fails, and expected inflation.

terms.plain: What a future payment is worth to you today, after shrinking it to account for the wait.
terms.formal: The current value of a future cash flow or series of cash flows, obtained by discounting them at an appropriate required rate of return.

terms.plain: What an amount of money today will have grown to by some later date, if it earns a return along the way.
terms.formal: The value of a present sum at a specified future date, given an assumed rate of return and compounding frequency.

terms.plain: The rate you use to shrink a future dollar down to what it is worth today. A higher rate means you value the future payment less.
terms.formal: The required rate of return used to convert future cash flows to present value, reflecting the time value of money and the risk of the cash flows.

terms.plain: A single number between 0 and 1 that you multiply a future payment by to get its value today. A factor of 0.75 means a future dollar is worth 75 cents now.
terms.formal: The quantity 1/(1+r)^n, which converts a cash flow received n periods from now into its present value at periodic discount rate r.

terms.plain: Earning returns on your returns. The interest you made last year starts earning interest of its own, which is why growth speeds up over long periods.
terms.formal: The process by which investment earnings are reinvested to generate additional earnings, producing exponential rather than linear growth over time.

terms.plain: The return you insist on before you would agree to make an investment, given how risky it is.
terms.formal: The minimum rate of return an investor demands to accept a given investment's risk, used as the discount rate when valuing its cash flows.

terms.plain: The return you can get with essentially no chance of losing your money — in practice, the yield on short-term government debt. It is the floor every other return is measured against.
terms.formal: The theoretical rate of return on an investment with zero default risk, commonly proxied by the yield on short-dated sovereign debt of a highly rated issuer.

terms.plain: A single percentage summarising the return on an investment whose cash flows arrive at irregular times. It is the discount rate that would make the investment exactly break even.
terms.formal: The discount rate at which the net present value of a series of cash flows equals zero. Sensitive to the timing of cash flows, which is why early distributions raise it.

terms.plain: Everything an investment will pay you, discounted to today's money, minus what it costs. Positive means it is worth doing.
terms.formal: The sum of all cash flows associated with an investment, each discounted to the present at the required rate of return, with outflows entered as negative.

terms.plain: A stream of identical payments at regular intervals — a lease, a bond's coupons, a pension. Because the payments are all the same, there is a one-line formula for its value.
terms.formal: A finite series of equal cash flows occurring at equal intervals. An ordinary annuity pays at the end of each period; the present value is PMT x (1-(1+r)^-n)/r.

terms.plain: An annuity whose payments arrive at the start of each period rather than the end — rent, insurance premiums. Every payment is one period closer, so it is worth (1+r) times an ordinary annuity.
terms.formal: An annuity in which cash flows occur at the beginning of each period. Its present value equals that of an otherwise identical ordinary annuity multiplied by (1+r).

terms.plain: A payment stream that never ends. Surprisingly, it is worth a finite amount: the payment divided by the rate. At 5%, a dollar forever is worth twenty dollars.
terms.formal: An infinite series of equal cash flows at equal intervals, with present value PMT/r. The growing form, PMT/(r-g), underpins most terminal value calculations.

terms.plain: The ordinary average: add everything up and divide by how many there are. Simple, and easily distorted by one extreme value.
terms.formal: The sum of observations divided by their count. For returns it estimates the expected return of a single randomly drawn period, and always equals or exceeds the geometric mean.

terms.plain: The average return that actually describes what happened to your money: the constant rate that, compounded, would have produced the same ending value.
terms.formal: The nth root of the product of (1+R) across n periods, less one. Always less than or equal to the arithmetic mean, with the gap widening as volatility rises.

terms.plain: The total growth over a whole period, not per year. Up 12.9% over three years is a cumulative return; about 4.1% a year is the annual equivalent.
terms.formal: The total percentage change in value over a multi-period horizon, computed by chaining growth factors: (1+R1)(1+R2)...(1+Rn) - 1.

terms.plain: A return that ignores when money moved in and out, so it measures the manager rather than the investor's timing. The standard for reporting liquid fund performance.
terms.formal: The geometric chaining of sub-period returns, each computed between cash flows, which removes the effect of contribution and withdrawal timing.

terms.plain: A return that weights each period by how much money was actually invested, so it captures both the manager's results and the timing of cash flows. In practice, usually an IRR.
terms.formal: The internal rate of return on an investor's actual cash flows, reflecting the size and timing of contributions and withdrawals as well as underlying performance.

terms.plain: The middle value when you sort the data. Unlike the average, it barely moves when one observation is extreme.
terms.formal: The value separating the higher half of a data set from the lower half. A robust measure of central tendency, insensitive to the magnitude of outliers.

terms.plain: The most frequently occurring value. Useful for categories, rarely useful for returns, which almost never repeat exactly.
terms.formal: The most frequent observation in a data set. A distribution may have more than one mode, or none meaningfully.

terms.plain: The average of the squared distances from the mean. Squaring stops positive and negative gaps cancelling, but it also makes big gaps count for much more.
terms.formal: The expected squared deviation from the mean. Its square root is the standard deviation; variances are additive over independent periods, which is why volatility scales with the square root of time.

terms.plain: The typical distance of an observation from the average, in the same units as the data. For returns it is called volatility.
terms.formal: The square root of the variance. For a sample, computed with n-1 in the denominator to correct for the mean having been estimated from the same data.

terms.plain: The data you actually have, as opposed to all the data that could exist. Five years of a fund's returns is a sample; every month it will ever produce is the population.
terms.formal: A subset of observations drawn from a population, used to estimate population parameters. Sample statistics carry estimation error measured by the standard error.

terms.plain: The complete set of everything you would want to measure, most of which you never get to see.
terms.formal: The entire collection of possible observations about which inference is sought. Population parameters are estimated from samples rather than observed directly.

terms.plain: When the failures drop out of your data, so what is left looks better than reality. Fund indices suffer badly from this: the funds that closed stop reporting.
terms.formal: A selection bias arising when entities that ceased to exist are excluded from a data set, systematically overstating the historical performance of the category.

terms.plain: The bell curve. Needs only a mean and a standard deviation to describe completely, which makes it convenient — and makes it badly wrong about extreme events.
terms.formal: A symmetric, two-parameter continuous distribution in which about 68%, 95% and 99.7% of observations fall within one, two and three standard deviations of the mean.

terms.plain: How many standard deviations an observation sits from the average. A z-score of -2 means unusually bad; about 2.3% of outcomes are worse, if the bell curve applies.
terms.formal: The standardised value (x - mean)/standard deviation, expressing an observation in units of standard deviation from the mean.

terms.plain: Whether a distribution is lopsided. Negative skew means mostly small gains with occasional severe losses — the shape of selling insurance.
terms.formal: The third standardised moment of a distribution, measuring asymmetry. Negative skew indicates a longer left tail; positive skew a longer right tail.

terms.plain: How much of the action is in the extremes. High kurtosis means more very large moves, in both directions, than a bell curve would produce.
terms.formal: The fourth standardised moment, measuring tail weight. A normal distribution has kurtosis 3; excess kurtosis is the amount above that.

terms.plain: Extreme outcomes happening far more often than a bell curve predicts. Markets do this reliably, which is why models built on the normal distribution fail exactly when it matters.
terms.formal: A distributional property, equivalent to positive excess kurtosis, in which extreme observations carry materially more probability than under a normal distribution of the same variance.

terms.plain: The chance of one thing given that another has already happened. Written P(A|B) and read "probability of A given B".
terms.formal: P(A|B) = P(A and B)/P(B), the probability of A restricted to outcomes in which B occurs. Not generally equal to P(B|A).

terms.plain: The chance of two things both happening. Only equal to multiplying the two individual chances when the events are genuinely unrelated.
terms.formal: P(A and B), the probability of the intersection of two events. Equals P(A) x P(B) if and only if the events are independent.

terms.plain: Two things where knowing one happened tells you nothing about the other. In finance this is usually assumed and usually false.
terms.formal: Events for which P(A|B) = P(A), equivalently P(A and B) = P(A) x P(B). Independence is an empirical claim, not a modelling convenience.

terms.plain: Two things that cannot both happen. Often confused with independent, which is nearly the opposite — mutually exclusive events are highly informative about each other.
terms.formal: Events with zero joint probability, so that the occurrence of one precludes the other. For such events P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B).

terms.plain: How common something is before you look at any evidence. The number people most often forget, and the one that usually decides the answer.
terms.formal: The unconditional prior probability of an event or characteristic in a population, prior to conditioning on any evidence.

terms.plain: The formula for updating a belief when evidence arrives. It combines how likely the evidence was with how likely the thing was to begin with.
terms.formal: P(A|B) = P(B|A) x P(A) / P(B), giving the posterior probability of a hypothesis given evidence, from the likelihood and the prior.

terms.plain: What you believed before seeing the new evidence.
terms.formal: The probability assigned to a hypothesis before conditioning on new data. Usually the base rate in the relevant population.

terms.plain: What you should believe after seeing the evidence, having properly accounted for how rare the thing was to start with.
terms.formal: The updated probability of a hypothesis after conditioning on observed data, obtained via Bayes' rule from the prior and the likelihood.

terms.plain: How much your estimate would wobble if you had drawn a different sample. It shrinks with the square root of the sample size, so precision is expensive.
terms.formal: The standard deviation of a sample statistic's sampling distribution. For a sample mean it is s/sqrt(n), falling only with the square root of observations.

terms.plain: A range around your estimate that reflects how uncertain it is. A wide interval containing zero means the data has not settled the question.
terms.formal: An interval constructed so that, over repeated sampling, a stated proportion of such intervals would contain the true parameter. Not a probability statement about the parameter itself.

terms.plain: The boring explanation you try to rule out — usually "the true value is zero" or "nothing is going on here".
terms.formal: The default hypothesis in a statistical test, typically of no effect, which the data may lead you to reject but can never confirm.

terms.plain: How often you would see a result this extreme if nothing were really going on. A small p-value means the boring explanation looks strained.
terms.formal: The probability, under the null hypothesis, of observing a test statistic at least as extreme as the one obtained. Not the probability that the null is true.

terms.plain: A result unlikely to have happened by chance. It says nothing about whether the effect is large enough to matter.
terms.formal: A finding whose p-value falls below a pre-specified threshold, conventionally 5%. Distinct from economic significance, and inflated by testing many hypotheses.

terms.plain: How many standard errors your estimate sits from zero. Above about 2 is the conventional bar for taking a result seriously.
terms.formal: The ratio of an estimate to its standard error, used to test whether the estimate differs from a hypothesised value. Roughly 1.96 corresponds to 5% significance in large samples.

terms.plain: How closely two things move together, on a scale from -1 to +1. Measures straight-line relationships only, which is why it can miss real exposures.
terms.formal: Covariance normalised by the product of the two standard deviations, bounded [-1, 1]. Captures linear association only, and is not stable across market regimes.

terms.plain: Whether two things tend to move in the same direction. The sign is meaningful; the size is not, because it depends on the units.
terms.formal: The expected product of two variables' deviations from their means. Scale-dependent, and normalised into correlation for comparability.

terms.plain: Fitting the best straight line through a scatter of two variables. In finance, regressing a fund on the market is where beta and alpha come from.
terms.formal: A model estimating the linear relationship between a dependent variable and one or more explanatory variables, typically by minimising the sum of squared residuals.

terms.plain: The share of one variable's movement that the model explains. For a fund regressed on the market, a high figure means the fund is mostly market movement.
terms.formal: The proportion of variance in the dependent variable explained by the regression. In a single-variable regression it equals the squared correlation.

terms.plain: The part of an observation the model failed to explain. Worth inspecting: if the residuals are largest in the worst months, the model is hiding the risk that matters.
terms.formal: The difference between an observed value and the value fitted by the model. In a market regression, the residual is the return not attributable to the market factor.
